title: Procurement strategy
blurb: Define procurement strategy: the high-level approach to securing goods and services from external suppliers.
question: A housing association needs a new tenant portal. It has no in-house developers, a firm budget, and wants the risk of cost overruns to sit with the supplier. Which document sets out its overall approach to getting this from the market?

teach.h: Getting what you won't do yourself
teach.body: Most projects need things they can't, or shouldn't, produce in-house: specialist software, steelwork, consultants, hired equipment. Before anyone signs a contract, the project decides HOW it will go to the market: whether to make or buy, how suppliers will be chosen, what kind of contract to use and who carries which risks. That overall approach is the procurement strategy.

Formally: a procurement strategy is the high-level approach for securing the goods and services required from external suppliers to satisfy project needs. Plainly: 'our game plan for buying in what we need.' It is strategic, so it sets direction for all the buying on the project, rather than being any single contract or purchase order.

teach.caption: Choosing the contract type is a risk decision: it decides who pays if the work costs more than expected.

steps.label: Award contracts
steps.sub: Each one in line with the strategy

teach.caption: The strategy comes first and shapes every contract that follows.

teach.body: The housing association has no developers, so it decides to buy. The core portal is well defined, so it chooses a fixed-price contract, putting overrun risk with the supplier. It runs a competitive tender judged on quality and price, pays at milestones such as 'portal live', and wants a longer-term partnership for support. Every one of those choices belongs in the procurement strategy.

items: Competitive tender: invite several suppliers to bid against set criteria.
Framework or approved list: choose from suppliers already vetted.
Single source: go direct to one supplier, e.g. the only one able to do the work.
Partnering: a longer-term, collaborative relationship with shared goals.

teach.text: A procurement strategy is the high-level APPROACH. It is not the contract itself, not just a list of supplier names, and not detailed delivery documents such as test scripts or a task list. It also concerns EXTERNAL suppliers: allocating your own staff is resource management, not procurement.

items: Procurement strategy: the high-level approach for securing goods and services from external suppliers.
Covers make or buy, supplier selection, contract type, risk allocation, payment and relationship.
Fixed price puts cost overrun risk mainly on the supplier; cost reimbursable puts it mainly on the buyer.
Set before contracts are let, and shapes every contract that follows.

summary: You can now define a procurement strategy as the high-level approach for securing goods and services from external suppliers. You can also list what it decides (make or buy, supplier selection, contract type, risk, payment and relationship) and tell it apart from an individual contract.

A.q: Which of the following best defines a procurement strategy?
options: The signed contract with a chosen supplier
The plan for assigning in-house staff
The approach to securing external supply
The list of approved suppliers to use
A.why: A procurement strategy is the high-level approach for securing goods and services from external suppliers.

whyNot.0: A contract is a single agreement that follows from the strategy.
whyNot.1: Assigning in-house staff is resource management, not procurement.
whyNot.3: An approved list may be one selection route, but it isn't the strategy.

A.q: Which of the following decisions belongs in a procurement strategy?
options: Whether to make or to buy
A.why: The make-or-buy decision is a core part of the procurement strategy.

whyNot.1: Board membership is a governance matter.
whyNot.3: PESTLE informs the context; it isn't a procurement decision.

A.q: Under a fixed-price contract, who mainly carries the risk of the work costing more than planned?
A.why: With a fixed price agreed up front, the supplier absorbs most of any cost overrun.

whyNot.0: The buyer carries most cost risk under cost-reimbursable contracts, not fixed price.
whyNot.2: End users don't carry contractual cost risk.
whyNot.3: The PMO supports standards and assurance; it doesn't bear contract cost risk.

B.q: The scope of some external design work is still very uncertain when it must start. Which contract type is most likely to suit?
B.why: Cost-reimbursable contracts pay actual costs plus a fee, which suits work whose scope is not yet clear.

whyNot.0: Fixed price suits well-defined scope; suppliers would price in heavy risk here.
whyNot.1: A lump sum is a form of fixed price, so it has the same problem.
whyNot.2: A firm price per item is still a fixed-price approach.

B.q: When is a procurement strategy normally produced?
B.why: The strategy sets the approach, so it must be agreed before going to the market and letting contracts.

whyNot.1: By then the key procurement decisions have already been made.
whyNot.2: Closure is far too late to shape how goods and services are obtained.
whyNot.3: It is needed on any project that buys externally, not only when things go wrong.

B.q:
Which TWO would you expect to find in a procurement strategy?
1. How suppliers will be selected
2. The detailed design of the product
3. The type of contract to be used
4. The team's Belbin roles
B.why: Supplier selection and contract type are central procurement strategy decisions.

whyNot.0: The detailed product design isn't part of a procurement strategy.
whyNot.1: Neither the product design nor Belbin roles belong in it.
whyNot.2: Belbin team roles relate to team building, not procurement.

C.q: A housing association has no in-house developers and a firm budget for a well-defined portal. Which procurement choice best fits?
options: Buy externally at a fixed price
C.why: No in-house skills points to buying, and a well-defined scope with a firm budget points to a fixed price.

whyNot.0: Without developers, making in-house isn't realistic.
whyNot.2: Cost reimbursable leaves the overrun risk with the buyer, which clashes with a firm budget.
whyNot.3: Delaying to hire staff ignores the option to buy and adds time.

C.q: Which of the following would a procurement strategy NOT normally set out?
options: How risk is shared with suppliers
C.why: Daily task lists are detailed delivery management, not part of the high-level procurement approach.

whyNot.0: The payment approach is a typical procurement strategy decision.
whyNot.1: Risk allocation with suppliers is a core part of the strategy.
whyNot.3: How suppliers will be selected is a core part of the strategy.

C.q: A hospital has no engineers of its own, and only one supplier in the country can maintain a specialist scanner. What might its procurement strategy decide?
C.why: With only one capable supplier and no in-house option, a single-source route is the sensible approach.

whyNot.0: An open tender is pointless when only one supplier can do the work.
whyNot.1: The hospital has no engineers, so making in-house isn't realistic.
whyNot.2: Resource smoothing balances internal resources; it isn't a procurement route.

reteach.title: Think of a house extension
reteach.question: You want a kitchen extension but you're not a builder. What do you decide before you sign anything?

blocks.h: Your plan for buying it in
blocks.body: You could project-manage it yourself and hire trades separately, or pay one builder to do everything. You could get three quotes or use the builder your neighbour recommends. You might agree a fixed price, or pay day rates because you don't yet know what's under the floor. You'd pay in stages as the walls and roof go up. Those decisions together are your procurement strategy.
A project's procurement strategy makes the same choices at a higher level, before any contract is signed, so all buying on the project follows one sensible approach.

explain.body: A procurement strategy is the high-level approach for securing goods and services from external suppliers. It shapes the contracts; it isn't one of them.

test.q: A procurement strategy is best described as which of these?
test.why: It is the overall approach to obtaining goods and services from external suppliers.

whyNot.0: A delivery schedule is a scheduling product.
whyNot.1: A signed agreement is a contract, which follows from the strategy.
whyNot.2: Supplier risks are recorded in the risk register.

explain.body: The first big choice: do the work in-house or buy it in? Missing skills, limited capacity and the chance to transfer risk favour buying; control and confidentiality may favour making.

options: The work is core and secret
test.why: If the organisation lacks the skills, buying them in from the market is the natural choice.

whyNot.0: Needing full control tends to favour making in-house.
whyNot.3: Core, confidential work is often kept in-house.

explain.body: Fixed price: the supplier carries most cost overrun risk, so it suits well-defined scope. Cost reimbursable: the buyer pays actual costs plus a fee and carries most of that risk, so it suits uncertain scope.

test.q: Under a cost-reimbursable contract, who carries most of the cost risk?
test.why: The buyer pays the actual costs plus a fee, so overruns fall mainly on the buyer.

whyNot.1: The supplier is paid its costs, so it carries little cost risk.
whyNot.2: End users aren't party to the contract.
whyNot.3: Regulators don't carry contract cost risk.

explain.body: The strategy also sets how suppliers are chosen (tender, framework, single source), how they are paid (for example at milestones) and the kind of relationship wanted, from one-off transaction to long-term partnership.

test.q: Choosing between a competitive tender and a single supplier is a decision about which of these?
test.why: How suppliers will be selected is one of the main elements of a procurement strategy.

whyNot.0: Contract closure happens at the end of a contract.
whyNot.1: Resource levelling balances resource demand against availability.
whyNot.3: Quality control checks outputs against requirements.
